## Big Question {.role-slide}

How well does a fitted model predict linguistic observations that did not contribute to its fit?

## Data {.role-slide}

A reading-time corpus repeats readers, passages, sentences, and word positions. A new row is not necessarily a new reader or a new passage.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Training fit rewards a model for adapting to the responses it has already seen. It does not measure prediction for omitted responses.

## This Module {.role-slide .compact}

1. State what must be new at prediction time.
2. Choose a loss and a validation split.
3. Compare models on matched omitted observations.
4. Relate predictive evaluation to likelihood-based criteria.

## What must be new at prediction time {.section-slide}

Naming the omitted observations

## Question {.role-slide}

Does the claim concern another response from represented units, a new participant, a new item, or a new passage?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Out-of-sample prediction**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) evaluates responses omitted during fitting. The omitted unit must match the claim.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 14</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

For prediction to a new passage, which rows must be absent during fitting, and which predictors would remain available?

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/prediction-targets.html)

## Predictive loss {.section-slide}

Defining the cost of an error

## Question {.role-slide}

Should a 40 ms miss count twice as much as a 20 ms miss, or four times as much?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Squared-error loss**](https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html) gives the 40 ms miss four times the loss. [**Absolute-error loss**](https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html) gives it twice the loss.

<div class="source">Wang, Probability and Statistical Theory</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The loss function determines what counts as a costly prediction error. The averaging unit determines whether rows or linguistic groups receive equal weight.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/predictive-loss.html)

## Prediction bias and prediction variance {.section-slide}

Error across repeated training samples

## Surprising Fact {.role-slide}

A flexible curve may follow the true frequency effect more closely on average while changing much more across possible corpora.

## Method {.role-slide}

The [**bias-variance decomposition**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) applies the earlier ideas of [estimator bias](../../statistical-inference/estimator-bias.html) and [estimator variance](../../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.html) to predictions.

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat f(x))^2
=\sigma^2+\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))^2+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f(x))
$$

<div class="source">James et al., Chapter 2</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Bias and prediction variance describe a complete learning procedure over repeated training samples. One observed corpus does not separately identify them.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/bias-variance-tradeoff.html)

## Training and test data {.section-slide}

Separating fitting from evaluation

## Idea {.role-slide}

The [**training set**](https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html) determines every fitted quantity. The [**test set**](https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html) is used only to evaluate the fitted procedure.

<div class="source">Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Section 5.9</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html
:::

## Challenge {.role-slide}

[**Data leakage**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage) occurs when test information influences a fitted decision. Centering, selection, and imputation must therefore be estimated within training data.

<div class="source">scikit-learn, Common pitfalls</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Split first. Then estimate every response-adaptive step on the training set and evaluate the prespecified procedure once on the test set.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.html)

## Cross-validation {.section-slide}

Rotating the separation

## Method {.role-slide}

[**K-fold cross-validation (CV)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) divides the data into folds and rotates which fold supplies the omitted responses.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 14</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Fit the complete procedure outside fold $k$.
2. Predict the responses in fold $k$.
3. Store predictions in their original rows.
4. Repeat until every row has one omitted-data prediction.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Cross-validation estimates the performance of the complete procedure. Every fitted transformation and selection decision belongs inside the rotation.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/cross-validation.html)

## Leaving out one unit at a time {.section-slide}

The meaning of one

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html) refits the procedure after omitting one specified unit at a time.

<div class="source">Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 14</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

If one unit is a trial, other trials from the same participant remain in training. Does that answer a new-participant question?

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The omitted unit is part of the statistical procedure. It cannot be inferred from the phrase “leave one out.”

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/leave-one-out-cross-validation.html)

## Grouped cross-validation {.section-slide}

Omitting complete linguistic units

## Data {.role-slide}

The Natural Stories Corpus contains word positions nested in sentences and stories, with responses repeated across readers.

<div class="source">Futrell et al. 2018</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://aclanthology.org/L18-1012/
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Grouped K-fold cross-validation**](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data) assigns all rows from one group to the same fold.

<div class="source">scikit-learn, Grouped data</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html#cross-validation-iterators-for-grouped-data
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Holding out complete readers tests prediction for absent readers. Holding out complete passages tests prediction for absent passages. These are different claims.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/grouped-cross-validation.html)

## Comparing predictive loss {.section-slide}

Pairing models on the same omitted groups

## Method {.role-slide}

For each held-out group $g$, compare paired losses with

$$
\Delta_g=L_{g,A}-L_{g,B}.
$$

Positive values favor Model B.

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

Report the aggregate difference, the proportion of groups that improve, and the distribution of group differences. Fold means are not independent replications.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A coefficient and a held-out loss difference answer different questions. The first describes a fitted association. The second describes predictive contribution under the chosen split.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/comparing-predictive-loss.html)

## Comparing nested likelihoods {.section-slide}

Likelihood-ratio tests

## Question {.role-slide}

Does a larger model improve maximized likelihood enough to reject the restrictions imposed by a nested smaller model?

## Method {.role-slide}

The [**likelihood-ratio test (LRT)**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=261) uses

$$
D=2\{\ell(\widehat\theta_1)-\ell(\widehat\theta_0)\}.
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 15</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=261
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The test concerns a specified nested restriction under its reference conditions. It is not an estimate of out-of-sample predictive performance.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/likelihood-ratio-tests.html)

## Penalizing in-sample fit {.section-slide}

Information criteria

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Akaike information criterion (AIC)**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) combines maximized fit with a parameter-count penalty.

$$
\mathrm{AIC}=-2\ell(\widehat\theta)+2k
$$

<div class="source">James et al., Chapter 6</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

[**Bayesian information criterion (BIC)**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) uses a penalty of $k\log n$. Its preferred model may differ from the AIC choice.

<div class="source">James et al., Chapter 6</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Information criteria compare models fit to the same responses. A raw difference is evidence only relative to the declared candidate set.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/information-criteria.html)

## Pareto-smoothed importance sampling {.section-slide}

Approximating Bayesian leave-one-out prediction

## Goal {.role-slide}

Compute each omitted response density under the [posterior](../../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.html) that would have been obtained without that response.

$$
p(y_i\mid y_{-i})=\int p(y_i\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid y_{-i})\,d\theta
$$

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO)**](https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html) approximates omitted posteriors using draws from the full posterior.

<div class="source">loo documentation</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://mc-stan.org/loo/articles/online-only/faq.html
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

The [**Pareto $k$ diagnostic**](https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html) evaluates the importance-sampling approximation. A large value does not establish that an observation should be deleted.

<div class="source">loo reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/pareto-k-diagnostic.html
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The resulting expected log pointwise predictive density remains tied to the unit represented by one likelihood contribution.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/psis-loo.html)

## The widely applicable information criterion {.section-slide}

A posterior-variance correction

## Idea {.role-slide}

[**Widely applicable information criterion (WAIC)**](https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html) subtracts a pointwise estimate of optimism from fitted posterior predictive density.

<div class="source">loo reference</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/waic.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

$$
\operatorname{elpd}_{\mathrm{waic}}
=\operatorname{lppd}
-\sum_i\operatorname{Var}_s\!\left[\log p(y_i\mid\theta^{(s)})\right]
$$

Larger values are preferred.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

WAIC uses the same pointwise log-likelihood matrix as PSIS-LOO, but its approximation is harder to diagnose when pointwise posterior variation is large.

[Return to the notes](../../model-criticism-and-prediction/waic.html)

## Conclusion {.section-slide}

Prediction beyond the fitted data

## Big Question {.role-slide}

How well does a fitted model predict linguistic observations that did not contribute to its fit?

## Answer {.role-slide .compact}

1. Name what is omitted and what remains available.
2. Choose a loss whose scale matches the scientific question.
3. Fit every adaptive step without the held-out responses.
4. Interpret comparison at the linguistic unit named by the claim.
